solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Battled healthy criminal? You'll be lucky!

indicators.note: criminal means crooked or wrong, so the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A fit young offender put up a fight, but his hopes of getting off are slim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'criminal' rearranges all fourteen letters of BATTLED HEALTHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are sceptical retorts expressing doubt that something hoped for will ever happen.

clue.text: Opening up every lunchtime in store shows real devotion

indicators.note: the three initials go inside the store

parts.note: a trove is a store or hoard of valuables

indicators.note: the opening of each word is its first letter

parts.note: the first letters of these three words are U, E and L

explanation.surface: A shop opening each lunchtime turns out to be a sign of real commitment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' takes UEL from the first letters of 'up every lunchtime', and 'in' puts them inside TROVE.
explanation.definitionFit: True love is genuine, deep affection, which is the same as real devotion.

clue.text: What dinner host may ask nowadays

definitions.meaning: first meaning: '...?', offering guests a second helping

explanation.walkthrough: The host's question 'Any more?' is written as one word to match the adverb meaning these days.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a host's offer of second helpings and an adverb meaning at the present time.

clue.text: Spindles I only partly wound

indicators.note: partly means only some of the letters are used, a stretch inside the words

parts.note: the answer runs through these words, across the word breaks

explanation.surface: Someone at a spinning wheel complains they only hurt themselves a little on the spindles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wound' looks like the past tense of wind, fitting the spindles, but it is the noun for an injury.
explanation.definitionFit: A lesion is an area of damaged tissue in the body, such as a cut, ulcer or injury.

clue.text: Request to take part in live attempts at wickerworks

indicators.note: taking part in means getting inside, so the request word goes within the word for live

parts.note: to be is to live or exist
to ask is to request
tries are attempts

explanation.surface: A person asks to join in the live trials of basket weaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take part in' puts ASK inside BE to give BASKE, and TRIES follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Basketry is the craft of weaving baskets, and its plural names pieces of woven wickerwork.

clue.text: You leave a content creator to listen to instrument

indicators.note: listening means hearing the word rather than seeing it, so what is left is entered by its sound

parts.note: a content creator is a YouTuber, who makes videos for YouTube; when you leave, the word loses its first three letters, giving the word said aloud

explanation.surface: You walk away from an online influencer to hear some music instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leave' drops YOU from YOUTUBER to leave TUBER, which 'to listen to' turns into the identical-sounding TUBA in a non-rhotic accent, as in British English.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the large, deep-voiced brass instrument at the bottom of the band.

clue.text: Scottish island contains real common

indicators.note: the island word holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: Eday is one of the Orkney Islands, off northern Scotland
very in its old sense means real or true, as in 'the very thing'

explanation.surface: An island off Scotland has genuine common land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' puts VERY inside EDAY. Eday is a small island in Orkney, a frequent crossword visitor.
explanation.definitionFit: Everyday means ordinary or commonplace, used or met with day in, day out.

clue.text: Falcons' home lacking a hunter

indicators.note: lacking means without, so one A is dropped from the name

parts.note: Atalanta is the huntress of Greek myth, famous for her speed

explanation.surface: A bird of prey's nest is without a predator to fear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking' removes an A from ATALANTA. The Falcons are Atlanta's American football team, so the 'home' is a city rather than a nest.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlanta, Georgia, is the home city of the Atlanta Falcons of the National Football League.

clue.text: Start to develop extremely dishy friend

parts.note: to bud is to begin to develop, as a plant does

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

parts.note: its first and last letters are D and Y

explanation.surface: A budding romance begins with a very attractive friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes the two end letters of 'dishy', which follow BUD.
explanation.definitionFit: Buddy is an informal word, chiefly American, for a friend or pal.

clue.text: Grant could be for classic work

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ... S. Grant, the American Civil War general and president, so Grant could be ...
second meaning: ..., James Joyce's modernist novel, or Homer's hero

explanation.surface: A grant might be made to fund work on a classic text.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like a sum of money, but it is the surname of US president Ulysses S. Grant.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's Ulysses is a landmark novel of 1922, and the name also belongs to President Grant.

clue.text: Silesian city — macabre slaughterhouses

parts.note: the answer runs across the join of these two words

explanation.surface: A city in central Europe is known for its grim abattoirs.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no signal word: the answer simply sits across the two words after the dash. Breslau is the German name for Wroclaw, now in Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: Breslau was the German name of Wroclaw, the historic capital of the region of Silesia.

clue.text: Check sweetheart's embracing acceptable second cousin

indicators.note: an embrace wraps around, so the lover word goes around the next pieces

parts.note: a lover is a sweetheart, and the 's stands for is

indicators.note: second picks the second letter of the word

parts.note: its second letter is O
OK means acceptable

explanation.surface: A girlfriend checks that it is fine to invite a second cousin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' takes O from 'cousin'; add OK, and 'embracing' puts OOK inside LOVER, just after its L.
explanation.definitionFit: To look something over is to examine or inspect it quickly, which is to check it.

clue.text: Celebrated that my end has started badly

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is H

indicators.note: done badly means done wrongly, so the letters of my end are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone celebrates the fact that their final chapter has got off to a poor start.
explanation.walkthrough: H, the start of 'has', comes first; 'badly' rearranges MY END into YMNED.
explanation.definitionFit: To hymn something is to praise it in song, so hymned means celebrated or extolled.

clue.text: Spending too much is obvious holding move

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so the word for move goes within the word for obvious

parts.note: overt means open and obvious
to budge is to move slightly

explanation.surface: Clearly a costly stalling tactic is blowing the budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding' puts BUDGE inside OVERT, between its R and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A project that is over budget has spent more than the amount allowed for it.

clue.text: Turning every unending turn

indicators.note: turning here means churning about, so the remaining letters are put in a new order
unending means with no end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A spinning motion keeps going round and round without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unending' cuts the Y off EVERY, and 'Turning' rearranges EVER. 'Turning' looks like the definition, but 'turn' at the end is.
explanation.definitionFit: To veer is to change direction suddenly, which is to turn aside.

clue.text: Started hole with a method that's outlawed

parts.note: in golf a hole is started by driving from the tee, so a golfer who started a hole drove
a way is a method

explanation.surface: Someone digging a hole has used a banned technique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Started hole' sounds like digging, but it is golf: each hole begins with a drive off the tee.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive someone away is to force them out, as an outlaw is banished from the community.

clue.text: Rich source of excitement

parts.note: a well is a source, of water or of anything
a to-do is a fuss or commotion, excitement

explanation.surface: A wealthy origin of thrills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rich' looks like an adjective describing the source, but it is the definition, and the rest splits into two plain pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-to-do means prosperous and comfortably off, which is wealthy.

clue.text: Hair in tonsorial centre is an aggravation

indicators.note: the hair word goes inside the next piece

parts.note: the middle three of the nine letters of tonsorial are S, O and R
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Hair styled in a barber's salon is a source of irritation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts TRESS inside SOR, the three letters at the centre of TONSORIAL. Tonsorial means to do with barbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A stressor is anything that causes stress, an irritant or aggravation.

clue.text: Trump — maybe cheer?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: when hearts are trumps, a player may trump a trick by taking it with a heart
second meaning: to cheer up, take courage and be encouraged

explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' suggests the politician, but it is the card-game sense: to take a trick with a card of the trump suit, such as a heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To take heart is to become encouraged and confident, so cheer in its sense of cheer up.

clue.text: Offensive fool gets no tip for poor service

indicators.note: gets here means acquires, so the fool word takes on the next piece after it

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: with no tip, a down word loses its top, its first letter

parts.note: a fault in tennis is a serve that fails, a poor service

explanation.surface: A rude idiot leaves the waiter nothing after bad service in a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no tip' cuts F off FAULT, a failed serve in tennis, to leave AULT after ASS. The restaurant picture of tipping is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault is an attack, a military offensive, so the noun matches the noun.

clue.text: Top batter exhausted

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to ... a score is to top it
second meaning: to batter, strike repeatedly
third meaning: ..., as in dead ..., worn out

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings of one short word sit side by side; 'Top batter' reads as a cricketer or baseball player, but the words separate.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to surpass, to strike repeatedly, and, as an adjective, worn out.

clue.text: Talk at length about being left out of drunken sex with pilot

indicators.note: drunken means staggering about, so the letters are mixed up
being left out of the mix means those letters are taken away from the pool

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange
taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone holds forth about being excluded from a boozy fling with an airline pilot.
explanation.walkthrough: SEX plus PILOT gives SEXPILOT; 'out of' takes away L (left), and 'drunken' rearranges what remains. 'being' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To exposit is to set out an explanation in detail, to expound on a subject at length.

clue.text: Hand in religious Christmas decoration

indicators.note: the hand letter goes inside the religious word

parts.note: holy means religious or sacred
L stands for left, as in the left hand

explanation.surface: Someone gives a hand with the decorations for a religious festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts L inside HOLY. A hand is left or right, so L is a hand here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprigs of holly, with prickly leaves and red berries, are a traditional seasonal decoration at Christmas.

clue.text: Section of orchestra taking A level

definitions.note: strata is the plural of stratum, but it is widely used loosely as a single layer, as here

indicators.note: a section is a part cut from something, so the answer is a run of letters within these words

parts.note: the answer spans the end of orchestra and the start of taking

explanation.surface: A part of the orchestra is sitting a school exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A level' looks like the English school-leaving exam, but it is the definition, with the answer used loosely as a singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Strata are layers of rock or tiers of society, each one a level.

clue.text: Tragically lose US fliers

indicators.note: done tragically means gone badly wrong, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sad farewell as American aviators are lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tragically' rearranges LOSE US. Ousels are birds of the thrush family, such as the ring ousel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ousels, also spelt ouzels, are thrush-like birds, so creatures that fly.

clue.text: Petrol's final extra input into hybrid's manifold

indicators.note: being input into something means being put inside it, so these pieces go within the hybrid

parts.note: a mule is a hybrid of a horse and a donkey

indicators.note: final picks the last letter of the word

parts.note: Petrol's is the word petrol, whose last letter is L
a tip is an extra paid for service

explanation.surface: Fuel and an additional boost feed into a hybrid car's engine manifold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'final' takes L from 'Petrol's', TIP follows, and 'input into' places LTIP inside MULE. 'manifold' looks like the engine part, but here it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Manifold as an adjective means many and various, which is what multiple means.

clue.text: For starters, where are your social manners?

indicators.note: starters are the first letters of each word

parts.note: the first letters of these four words are W, A, Y and S

explanation.surface: A dinner guest is asked, before the starters arrive, where their social graces have gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For starters' suggests the first course of a meal, but it takes the first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ways are customs and manners, as in 'the ways of polite society'.

clue.text: Currency leads to oblivion from lack of transparency

parts.note: the leu is the currency of Romania and Moldova
a coma is a state of deep unconsciousness, oblivion

explanation.surface: Money ends in obliteration because the finances are opaque.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leads to' is a link joining the pieces. Leucoma is a white opacity of the cornea, so the eye loses its transparency.
explanation.definitionFit: Leucoma is a dense white clouding of the cornea that makes it opaque instead of clear.

clue.text: Good girls may be shot

parts.note: lasses are girls, especially in northern England and Scotland

explanation.surface: Even well-behaved girls could end up being shot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be shot' sounds menacing, but a shot glass is one kind of glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A shot glass is a small glass for a single measure of spirits, so glasses may be shot glasses.

clue.text: Never mind inmates trotted out

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Don't worry that the prisoners jogged off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges INMATES TROTTED.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are dismissive ways of saying something is of no importance and can be ignored.
